claims.text: The 15–45 μm FeCoNiCrAl feedstock produces a bond coat thinner than required.
Replacing 15–45 μm feedstock with 45–100 μm feedstock will increase the deposited bond-coat thickness.
The larger feedstock will preserve coating integrity.
The larger feedstock will maintain minimal as-sprayed oxidation.
Larger particles have a lower surface-to-volume ratio than smaller particles.
The lower surface-to-volume ratio of larger particles limits oxidation during flight.
Larger particles carry higher momentum upon impact under the proposed spray conditions.
Particle impact in cold spray can lead to consolidation and bonding.
Higher impact momentum from larger particles improves particle bonding and coating densification.
Improved bonding and densification increase deposition efficiency.
Increased deposition efficiency produces faster coating-thickness buildup.
The 45–100 μm feedstock will produce a statistically significant thickness increase over the 15–45 μm baseline.
The thicker coating will retain microstructural cohesion and will not have higher oxidation than the baseline.
The intervention should remain effective under standard thermal-spray settings and typical thermal-barrier bond-coat service temperatures and loads.
The effectiveness of the larger powder may depend on adjusting deposition parameters to account for its kinetic and melting behavior.
Larger powder may introduce microstructural inhomogeneity, altered melting dynamics, reduced adhesion, or impaired long-term performance.
Cold spray is part of the thermal-spray process family.
A controlled comparison holding the other deposition parameters constant can test whether particle size changes thickness, oxidation, and microstructural integrity.
Failure to increase thickness significantly, or an increase in oxidation or microstructural damage, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The proposal calls for using the same operating parameters in the controlled test, while also stating that larger particles may require precise parameter adjustment or fine-tuning. Thus, the specified test may not evaluate the intervention under the conditions claimed to be necessary for its effectiveness.
